subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Illusion of Knowledge
description: A 60-second lesson on Illusion of Knowledge.

hook.text: Traders with more data made worse predictions than those with less. More information felt like more skill.

buildup.text: Paul Slovic gave horse bettors 5 facts, then 40. Their accuracy stayed flat but confidence doubled.

discovery.text: Extra information increases confidence faster than it increases accuracy. The gap is the illusion.

twist.text: Experts are most vulnerable. Specialists drown in data and mistake familiarity for understanding.

climax.text: Before deciding, ask: does this new data change my prediction or just my confidence? Test honestly.

punchline.text: More data is not more wisdom. Know the difference.

quiz.question: What happened when bettors received more data in Slovic's study?
options: Confidence rose but accuracy stayed flat

details.summary: The illusion of knowledge occurs when access to information creates the feeling of understanding even when the information has not been comprehended. Having data available makes people feel informed regardless of whether they have actually processed and understood it.
details.whyItMatters: In the information age, access to information is confused with understanding of it. Decision-makers surrounded by dashboards and reports feel knowledgeable but may understand less than someone who deeply processed a fraction of the same information.
takeaways: Access to information creates false confidence in understanding
More data does not automatically mean better decisions
Deep processing of less information often outperforms shallow access to more

faq.question: How does having more information sometimes lead to worse decisions?
faq.answer: Additional information increases confidence more than accuracy. People feel more justified in their decisions but the extra data creates noise that obscures the signal. The sweet spot is enough information to identify the key factors, deeply understood.

faq.question: How can decision-makers avoid the illusion of knowledge?
faq.answer: Test your understanding by explaining conclusions without looking at the data. If you cannot, you have access but not understanding. Focus on few key metrics that you deeply comprehend rather than many that you merely glance at.
